newsitem.title: USA: Ford sees $150 mln charge from vehicle actions.
newsitem.headline: Ford sees $150 mln charge from vehicle actions.

text.p: Ford Motor Co's decision to discontinue production of four vehicles will most likely result in a second quarter charge of about $150 million, Ford Automotive Operations President Jacques Nasser said Monday.

The one-time charge, which Nasser estimated at $150 million, would cover the cost of discontinuing three car lines -- the Mercury Cougar, Ford Thunderbird and Ford Probe -- and the Ford Aerostar minivan.
It does not include any ongoing costs, which is still being determined, Nasser said during a conference call with reporters.

Nasser said Ford plans to keep the passenger car assembly plant at its Lorain, Ohio, facility, but has not made a final decision on how it will be utilized. Options include using it to produce components or other assemblies.
"We may be able to do other things in the plant, and we're looking at that," Nasser said. "But at this point, (we have) no specific plans."
Ford plans to bring the Thunderbird back as a specialty sports coupe, but has not made a final decision on what will happen to the Mercury Cougar, Nasser said.
Nasser said Ford's Auto Alliance joint venture with Mazda Motor Motor Corp in Flat Rock, Mich., will produce a new Ford product, but he declined to elaborate.

In a press release, Ford did not specify what will be made at Flat Rock, saying only that production of 1998 models for Mazda will begin in September. Industry analysts have said Ford will make a Cougar replacement at the plant.

Nasser characterized the decision to drop the vehicles as necessary if the U.S. No. 2 automaker wants to keep up with the market place shift away from cars. More than 55 percent of Ford's U.S. production is now in the light truck segment, which includes pickup trucks, minivans and sport utility vehicles, he said.
"I think on balance I'm reasonably confident we've got the mix right now," he said. "The marketplace will let us know."
Nasser added: "I'd be surpised if we had any further major changes (in the U.S.) over the next couple of years."
